title: The Man Reviving Left Antisemitism
author: Michael C. Behrent
content:
![The Man Reviving Left
Antisemitism](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/09/AP26162567737529.jpg)

> _LFI: Anatomie d 'une perversion _  
> Edited by Pierre-Andre Taguieff  
> David Reinharc, 424 pages, $26

We live in an age of inversions. With class inversion, college-educated
professionals have moved inexorably leftwards, while once left-leaning blue-
collar workers have veered to the right. A few years ago, there was also talk
of a demographic inversion, as affluent populations that used to be drawn to
the suburbs moved back to cities. However, few inversions have been as
striking as the shifting political valences of antisemitism. In her
contribution to Pierre-Andre Taguieff's new edited volume on left antisemitism
in France, sociologist Eva Illouz describes it this way: "Today, the heirs of
Petain defend the Jews while the [radical] left has become antisemitic." The
National Rally, the party whose founder Jean-Marie Le Pen was repeatedly
convicted for making antisemitic remarks, positions itself as a defender of
Israel and French Jews, while _La France Insoumise_ (LFI, or Unbowed France),
the largest left-wing party, has moved in the other direction.

LFI's leader, Jean-Luc Melenchon, has achieved the rare feat of becoming
France's most controversial politician, a title long held first by Le Pen,
then by his daughter Marine, whom Melenchon could well face in the runoff of
next year's presidential election. He has done this in part through his
propensity to make comments that test the boundary between criticism of Israel
and outright antisemitism. In the pages of Taguieff's book, the Jewish
essayist Alain Finkiekraut says of LFI: "For the first time in my life, I am
afraid, physically afraid of a political party."

Taguieff's new volume mobilizes the energies of nearly sixty intellectuals to
expose Melenchon's party as a political "perversion." Though it considers LFI
from multiple angles--extremism, the politics of victimhood, a predilection
for "deconstruction"--many of the essays zero in on LFI's attitude to Jews.
Taguieff, a philosopher who studies racism and anti-Semitism, is known for
documenting the rise of a "[_new
Judeophobia_](https://www.amazon.com/dp/1566635713?lv=shuf&channelId=500&plpRedirect=mhFallback&ref=compactmag.com)"
in France, associated not with the far right but with French Muslims and
hostility to Israel. Taguieff's work is controversial. Some accuse him of
conflating antisemitism and anti-Zionism, and even of exemplifying the racism
he criticizes.

Taguieff's book stands in the tradition of what the French call _livres noirs_
--"black books" that present the dark side of a political phenomenon. Yet
while it documents many of LFI's most troubling features, it also explores the
reasons for left-wing antisemitism's emergence. It raises the question: Why,
in 2026, has the Jewish question become central to the left's current
identity?
